report:
## Conclusion

Yes — the evidence strongly supports that EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) is effective at reducing PTSD symptoms. Multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses show clinically meaningful, often large, reductions in PTSD symptoms with EMDR, and its efficacy is generally comparable to trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapies (TF-CBT), such as prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy.

A recent meta-analysis (Yunitri et al., 2023) pooling data from 98 RCTs (5,567 participants) found EMDR and cognitive processing therapy produced the strongest, moderate-to-large long-term effects on PTSD symptoms (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37882423). Systematic reviews since 2013 similarly conclude that EMDR's efficacy for adult PTSD is equivalent to TF-CBT approaches (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_movement_desensitization_and_reprocessing). This equivalence is echoed by a Cochrane-referenced review, which found EMDR and trauma-focused CBT "equally effective" for PTSD treatment, though it noted some methodological limitations in the underlying studies that warrant cautious interpretation (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK73148).

Clinical guideline bodies have also endorsed EMDR: the American Psychological Association's clinical practice guideline includes EMDR as a recommended treatment (conditionally, in the updated 2025 revision), and the World Health Organization has recommended EMDR alongside CBT for trauma-related mental health conditions following its 2013 guidance review (apa.org/ptsd-guideline/treatments/eye-movement-reprocessing; who.int/news/item/06-08-2013-who-releases-guidance-on-mental-health-care-after-trauma).

**Bottom line:** EMDR is a well-supported, evidence-based treatment that can significantly alleviate PTSD symptoms, with effectiveness broadly on par with established trauma-focused CBT approaches, and it is endorsed by major clinical and international health bodies.

- https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK73148/
